title: The Cardiovascular System
description: Week 10, matched to the instructor's Exam 4 study guide: blood flow through the heart, its valves, chambers, and membranes, the ECG's waves, blood components and blood type compatibility, capillary refill and arterial and venous insufficiency, thrombus, aneurysm, heart attack, murmurs, and stroke, autonomic control of the heart and blood pressure, heart-healthy habits, metabolic syndrome, and the risk factors for cardiovascular disease, with a case study.

legpain.intro: A nurse at a primary care clinic is assessing a 66-year-old client who reports pain in the left leg.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.html:
Nurses' Notes

1030: Client reports cramping pain in the left calf after walking about 2 blocks, which eases after a few minutes of rest. Smokes 1 pack a day. Has type 2 diabetes. Left foot cool, pale, and shiny, with no hair; thick toenails. Weak (1+) pulse on top of the left foot. Capillary refill 4 seconds in the left toes, 2 seconds in the right toes. No swelling in either leg. A small, round sore with a pale base on the left little toe.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how blood leaves the heart. Click the chamber that pumps oxygen-rich blood out to the body.
questions.alt: Front view of a heart cut open to show its inside, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: two upper chambers and two lower chambers, all the same color, with a valve between each upper and lower chamber; a large vein entering the upper chamber on the viewer's left from above and another from below; two veins entering the upper chamber on the viewer's right from the side; and two large arteries rising from the lower chambers and crossing, one of them arching over the top of the heart.
questions.rationale:
The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, which carries it to the body. On a front view, the client's left is on the viewer's right, so it's the lower chamber on the viewer's right. Its wall is the thickest in the heart because it pumps against the high pressure of the systemic circulation.

The right ventricle, the lower chamber on the viewer's left, pumps oxygen-poor blood into the pulmonary trunk, toward the lungs. The two upper chambers, the atria, receive blood: the right atrium from the venae cavae, and the left atrium from the pulmonary veins.

Takeaway: The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta; on a front view, it's the lower chamber on the viewer's right.

questions.stem: Blood that is low in oxygen returns from the body to the heart through the venae cavae. Place the structures in the order that blood passes through them on its way to the aorta.
questions.rationale:
Blood from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae, passes the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle, and is pumped through the pulmonic valve into the pulmonary trunk and pulmonary arteries to the lungs (the pulmonary circulation). In the lungs, it picks up oxygen and gives off carbon dioxide. The pulmonary veins carry the oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium; it passes the mitral valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it through the aortic valve into the aorta and out to the body (the systemic circulation).

Common mistakes are sending blood from the right side straight to the left side, skipping the lungs, and mixing up the pulmonary arteries, which carry blood away from the heart to the lungs, with the pulmonary veins, which bring it back.

Putting the pulmonary veins before the pulmonary arteries is a mistake: arteries carry blood away from the heart, to the lungs, and veins bring it back.

Takeaway: Right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the valves of the heart. For each valve, click to specify where it is.
columns: Between the left ventricle and the aorta
Between the right atrium and right ventricle
Between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery
Between the left atrium and left ventricle
questions.rationale:
The two atrioventricular (AV) valves sit between each atrium and its ventricle: the tricuspid valve on the right (right atrium to right ventricle) and the mitral valve on the left (left atrium to left ventricle). Cords called chordae tendineae tie their leaflets to the papillary muscles of the ventricles, so the leaflets don't flip back into the atria.

The two semilunar valves sit where the arteries leave the ventricles: the pulmonic valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery, and the aortic valve between the left ventricle and the aorta.

The pulmonic and aortic valves are the pair most often switched: the pulmonic valve opens from the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery.

Takeaway: The tricuspid and mitral valves are the AV valves (atrium to ventricle); the pulmonic and aortic valves are the semilunar valves (ventricle to artery).

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the layers of the heart wall. Which of the following layers contracts to pump blood?
options: Myocardium
Endocardium
Epicardium
Fibrous pericardium
questions.rationale:
The myocardium, the middle and thickest layer, is cardiac muscle; its cells contract to pump blood.

The endocardium is the thin inner lining of the chambers and valves; the conduction system runs just beneath it. The epicardium is the outer layer of the heart wall (the visceral layer of the pericardium), where the coronary arteries and veins run. The fibrous pericardium is the tough outer layer of the sac around the heart; it protects and anchors the heart but doesn't contract.

Takeaway: Myo- means muscle: the myocardium is the heart wall's muscle layer, the one that pumps.

questions.stem: A client's right ventricle is no longer pumping effectively. Which of the following describes where blood backs up first?
options: Into the veins that bring blood from the lungs
Into the arteries that carry blood to the body
Into the veins that bring blood from the body
Into the arteries that carry blood to the lungs
questions.rationale:
Blood reaches the right ventricle from the right atrium, which collects it from the body through the venae cavae. When the right ventricle can't pump all of it forward into the pulmonary arteries, blood backs up behind it: into the right atrium and the veins that bring blood from the body, where the pressure rises.

Backup into the veins from the lungs (the pulmonary veins) happens when the left ventricle fails, since the lungs drain into the left side of the heart. The arteries to the lungs and the arteries to the body are downstream of the ventricles: blood is pumped into them, so it doesn't back up into them.

“Into the veins that bring blood from the lungs” isn't the right answer: backup sounds like the lungs, but that's left-sided failure; a failing right ventricle backs blood up into the veins from the body.

Takeaway: Blood backs up behind a failing ventricle: right-sided failure backs up into the veins from the body, and left-sided failure backs up into the lungs.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the cardiac cycle. For each event, click to specify whether it happens during ventricular diastole or ventricular systole.
rows: The aortic and pulmonic valves are open
The mitral and tricuspid valves are open
Blood is pushed into the aorta and pulmonary arteries
questions.rationale:
Ventricular diastole is relaxation and filling: the ventricular muscle relaxes, the mitral and tricuspid valves are open, and the ventricles fill with blood from the atria. It begins when the aortic and pulmonic valves close and ends when the mitral and tricuspid valves close.

Ventricular systole is contraction and ejection: once the pressure in the ventricles rises above the pressure in the arteries, the aortic and pulmonic valves open, and blood is pushed into the aorta and pulmonary arteries. It begins when the mitral and tricuspid valves close and ends when the aortic and pulmonic valves close.

For the valve rows, the mitral and tricuspid valves are open while the ventricles fill (diastole), and the aortic and pulmonic valves open when the ventricles pump (systole).

Takeaway: Diastole: ventricles relax and fill, AV valves open. Systole: ventricles contract and eject, semilunar valves open.

questions.topic: Coronary circulation and the cardiac cycle
questions.stem: A client's blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg. Which of the following does the 84 represent?
options: The peak pressure in the arteries while the ventricles contract
The difference between the systolic and diastolic pressures
The average pressure in the arteries over the whole cardiac cycle
The lowest pressure in the arteries while the ventricles relax and fill
questions.rationale:
Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic. The diastolic pressure (84) is the lowest pressure in the arteries, while the ventricles relax and fill (ventricular diastole); the elastic aorta, recoiling after each beat, keeps it from falling further. The systolic pressure (136) is the peak pressure, while the ventricles contract and eject blood.

The difference between them (136 − 84 = 52 mm Hg) is the pulse pressure. The average pressure over the whole cycle is the mean arterial pressure (MAP), which is always closer to the diastolic pressure.

Takeaway: The bottom number is the diastolic pressure: the lowest pressure in the arteries, while the ventricles fill.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the conduction system of the heart. Click the structure that normally starts each heartbeat.
questions.alt: Front view of a heart cut open to show its four chambers, with the client's right on the viewer's left, marked R and L: a large vein entering the upper chamber on the viewer's left from above and another from below, two veins entering the upper chamber on the viewer's right, a valve between each upper and lower chamber, and yellow structures in the walls of the heart: two yellow ovals, a short yellow band, and yellow lines running down the wall between the lower chambers and up along their outer walls.
questions.rationale:
The sinoatrial (SA) node, in the wall of the right atrium near where the superior vena cava enters, is the heart's natural pacemaker. Its pacemaker cells fire on their own, normally 60 to 100 times a minute, which sets a normal sinus rhythm; the autonomic nervous system speeds it up or slows it down. Each impulse spreads through the atria and makes them contract.

The atrioventricular (AV) node, the yellow oval low in the wall between the atria, receives the impulse and delays it briefly. The bundle of His, the bundle branches, and the Purkinje fibers then carry it through the ventricles. None of them starts the beat when the SA node is working.

Takeaway: The SA node, high in the right atrium, starts each normal heartbeat, 60 to 100 times a minute.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a normal ECG. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: On an ECG, the P wave shows {{0}}, the QRS complex shows {{1}}, and the T wave shows {{2}}.
questions.rationale:
The P wave, the first wave, is atrial depolarization, which starts at the SA node just before the atria contract. The QRS complex is ventricular depolarization: the Q wave is the septum, the R wave is the main mass of the ventricles (they contract at its peak), and the S wave is the last of the Purkinje fibers. The T wave is ventricular repolarization.

The AV node's delay is part of the PR interval, the time from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex (120 to 200 ms); it isn't a wave of its own. Atrial repolarization happens at the same time as the QRS complex, so it doesn't show as a separate wave.

The T wave isn't the right answer: it shows ventricular repolarization; atrial repolarization is hidden in the QRS complex.

Takeaway: P = the atria depolarize; QRS = the ventricles depolarize; T = the ventricles repolarize.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a client's ECG: heart rate 78/min, an upright P wave before each QRS complex, PR interval 160 ms, and QRS complex 140 ms. Which of the following findings should the nurse report to the provider?
options: Heart rate of 78/min
PR interval of 160 ms
QRS complex of 140 ms
Upright P wave before each QRS complex
questions.rationale:
A normal QRS complex lasts less than 120 ms (usually 60 to 100 ms), because the impulse spreads quickly through the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers. At 140 ms, this client's QRS is wide, so the ventricles are depolarizing slowly or by an abnormal path, as with a bundle branch block, a high potassium level, or a rhythm that starts in the ventricles. It needs follow-up.

A PR interval of 160 ms is within the normal 120 to 200 ms, so the AV node's delay is normal. A heart rate of 78/min is within 60 to 100, and an upright P wave before each QRS complex shows that each beat starts in the SA node.

The PR interval of 160 ms isn't the right answer: intervals are easy to mix up, but it's normal; a QRS over 120 ms is wide.

Takeaway: PR interval 120 to 200 ms; QRS under 120 ms. A wider QRS means slow or abnormal spread through the ventricles.

questions.stem: During a sympathetic (fight-or-flight) response, a client's arteries narrow and the blood pressure rises. Which of the following layers of the artery wall narrows the artery?
options: Tunica media
Tunica intima
Tunica externa
External elastic membrane
questions.rationale:
The tunica media, the middle layer, is mostly smooth muscle. When the sympathetic nervous system stimulates it, the muscle contracts and the artery narrows (vasoconstriction), which raises resistance and blood pressure; when the muscle relaxes, the artery widens. The media is thickest on the arterial side, and in small arteries and arterioles, it controls resistance.

The tunica intima, the inner layer, is a single layer of endothelial cells on a basal lamina, in contact with the blood. The tunica externa (adventitia), the outer layer, is mostly collagen that keeps the vessel intact and anchors it, and it carries the vessel's own blood vessels and nerves (the vasa vasorum and nervi vasorum). The external elastic membrane is a layer of elastic fibers between the media and the externa; it doesn't contract.

Takeaway: The smooth muscle of the tunica media changes a blood vessel's diameter.

questions.stem: A client's red blood cell count is below the expected range. Which of the following functions is most affected?
options: Fighting bacterial infections
Carrying oxygen to the tissues
Forming clots to stop bleeding
Holding fluid inside the blood vessels
questions.rationale:
Red blood cells (erythrocytes), about 4 to 6 million in each mm³ of blood, are full of hemoglobin, which carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues; they also help return carbon dioxide to the lungs. They're made in the red bone marrow and live about 120 days. With fewer of them, less oxygen reaches the tissues, which can cause fatigue and shortness of breath with activity.

Fighting infections is the job of the white blood cells, forming clots the job of the platelets and clotting proteins such as fibrinogen, and holding fluid in the vessels depends mainly on the plasma protein albumin.

Takeaway: Red blood cells carry oxygen on hemoglobin, so a low count means less oxygen for the tissues.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the types of white blood cells. For each description, click to specify the white blood cell it describes.
rows: Makes antibodies, and some live for years as memory cells
Rises first in an acute bacterial infection
Rises in chronic infections and becomes a macrophage in the tissues
Releases heparin, which helps prevent clotting
questions.rationale:
Neutrophils are the first responders in an acute (sudden) bacterial infection, and they live from hours to a few days. Eosinophils fight parasites and take part in allergic reactions. Basophils take part in allergic reactions and release heparin, which helps prevent clotting. These three are the granulocytes. The agranulocytes are the lymphocytes, which make antibodies (B cells) and include memory cells that live for years, and the monocytes, which rise in chronic infections and become macrophages in the tissues.

The neutrophil and monocyte rows are the pair most often switched: neutrophils rise first in an acute bacterial infection; monocytes rise in chronic infections and become macrophages.

Takeaway: Neutrophils: acute infection. Eosinophils: parasites and allergy. Basophils: allergy and heparin. Lymphocytes: antibodies. Monocytes: chronic infection.

questions.stem: A client's platelet count is very low. Which of the following findings should the nurse monitor for?
options: Bleeding gums
Fever and frequent infections
Easy bruising
Nosebleeds
Fatigue and shortness of breath
Blood in the urine
questions.rationale:
Platelets (thrombocytes) are small cell fragments without a nucleus. They're made in the bone marrow, live 7 to 10 days, and plug damaged vessels to start clotting. With very few platelets, small injuries keep bleeding, so the nurse watches for bleeding gums, easy bruising, nosebleeds, and blood in the urine.

Fever and frequent infections point to a problem with the white blood cells, and fatigue and shortness of breath to a problem with the red blood cells.

Fatigue and shortness of breath don't fit a low platelet count: they come with blood problems, but they point to too few red blood cells (anemia), not platelets.

Takeaway: A low platelet count means a risk of bleeding: check the gums, skin, nose, and urine.

questions.stem: A client with liver failure has a low albumin level and new swelling in both legs. Which of the following explains the swelling?
options: Less albumin makes the blood clot more easily
Less albumin blocks the client's lymphatic vessels
Less albumin raises the pressure in the client's arteries
Less albumin lets fluid move out of the blood vessels
questions.rationale:
Albumin, the main protein in plasma, is made by the liver. It keeps fluid inside the blood vessels by osmotic pressure: it draws water into the blood. When the liver fails and the albumin level drops, less water is held in the vessels, so fluid moves out into the tissues and causes swelling (edema), often in the legs.

Clotting depends on platelets and clotting proteins such as fibrinogen, not albumin. A low albumin level doesn't block lymphatic vessels, and it doesn't raise the pressure in the arteries.

“Less albumin blocks the lymphatic vessels” isn't the right answer: blocked lymph also causes swelling, but albumin's job is to hold fluid inside the blood vessels.

Takeaway: Albumin holds fluid in the vessels; a low albumin level lets fluid leak into the tissues as edema.

questions.stem: A client with type A-negative blood needs a transfusion of red blood cells. Which of the following donor blood types is compatible?
options: O-negative
A-positive
B-negative
AB-negative
questions.rationale:
Type A blood has the A antigen on its red blood cells and anti-B antibodies in its plasma, so the client can receive red blood cells without the B antigen: type A or type O. The client is also Rh-negative, with no Rh factor on the red blood cells, so the cells given should be Rh-negative too. O-negative red blood cells have no A, B, or Rh antigens, so they're compatible (A-negative cells would be too).

A-positive cells carry the Rh factor, which an Rh-negative client can make antibodies against. B-negative and AB-negative cells carry the B antigen, which the client's anti-B antibodies would attack.

A-positive isn't the right answer: it matches the A, but an Rh-negative client should receive Rh-negative red cells; O-negative works for any recipient's red cells.

Takeaway: Donor red cells must not carry an antigen the client lacks: A, B, or the Rh factor.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to give red blood cell transfusions to 4 clients. Which of the following transfusions should the nurse clarify with the provider?
options: Type B-negative cells for a client with type B-positive blood
Type A-negative cells for a client with type AB-positive blood
Type B-positive cells for a client with type A-positive blood
Type O-positive cells for a client with type O-positive blood
questions.rationale:
A client can safely receive red blood cells only if the cells carry no A, B, or Rh antigen that the client's own cells lack, since the client's antibodies would attack it. A client with type A-positive blood has anti-B antibodies, so type B-positive cells, which carry the B antigen, aren't compatible. The nurse should clarify this transfusion before giving it.

The other transfusions are compatible. B-negative cells carry the B antigen and no Rh factor, and a B-positive client has both. A-negative cells carry only the A antigen, and an AB-positive client has A, B, and Rh antigens and no anti-A or anti-B antibodies. O-positive cells carry only the Rh factor, which an O-positive client has too.

B-negative cells for a B-positive client don't need clarifying: the Rh doesn't match, but Rh-negative cells are safe for an Rh-positive client; giving type B cells to a type A client is the dangerous mismatch.

Takeaway: Before a transfusion, check that the donor's red cells carry no antigen the client lacks: A, B, or Rh.

questions.topic: Regulation of blood pressure and blood gases
questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing how the body senses blood pressure. Which of the following locations contain the baroreceptors that monitor arterial blood pressure?
options: The medulla oblongata and pons
The carotid sinus and aortic arch
The kidneys and adrenal glands
The hypothalamus and pituitary gland
questions.rationale:
Baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch. They sense how much the artery walls stretch and signal the vasomotor center in the medulla oblongata within seconds, through the glossopharyngeal nerve from the carotid sinus and the vagus nerve from the aortic arch.

The medulla oblongata receives the signals and responds, but it doesn't sense arterial pressure itself. The kidneys respond to low blood flow by releasing renin, and the adrenal glands release epinephrine, norepinephrine, and aldosterone, which raise the pressure over minutes to hours. The hypothalamus and pituitary gland make and release ADH (vasopressin), which also acts more slowly.

Takeaway: Baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense blood pressure and report to the medulla.

questions.stem: A client who is bleeding has a falling blood pressure. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: As the blood pressure falls, the baroreceptors send fewer signals to the {{0}}, which responds by increasing {{1}} activity. This {{2}} blood vessels, raising the blood pressure.

options: hypothalamus
medulla oblongata
cerebellum
pituitary gland
sympathetic
parasympathetic
somatic
slows the heart rate and widens
speeds up the heart rate and narrows
slows the heart rate and narrows
speeds up the heart rate and widens

questions.rationale:
Baroreceptors sense the stretch of the artery walls. When the blood pressure falls, they're stretched less and send fewer signals to the vasomotor center in the medulla oblongata. The medulla responds by increasing sympathetic activity and decreasing parasympathetic activity, which speeds up the heart rate, strengthens each contraction, and narrows the blood vessels (vasoconstriction), raising the blood pressure within seconds.

The parasympathetic system does the opposite when the pressure is high: it slows the heart and widens the vessels. The somatic system controls skeletal muscle, not the heart or vessels. The hypothalamus, cerebellum, and pituitary gland aren't the center for this reflex.

The parasympathetic choice isn't the right answer: falling pressure means fewer baroreceptor signals, which increases sympathetic activity.

Takeaway: Low blood pressure → fewer baroreceptor signals → the medulla raises sympathetic activity → faster heart rate and narrower vessels.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the arterial blood gas and electrolyte results of a 72-year-old client: pH 7.34, PaCO₂ 46 mm Hg, PaO₂ 78 mm Hg, and K⁺ 6.3 mmol/L. Which of the following results should the nurse report to the provider first?
options: PaCO₂ 46 mm Hg
PaO₂ 78 mm Hg
Potassium 6.3 mmol/L
questions.rationale:
A potassium level of 6.3 mmol/L is above both the normal range (3.5 to 5.0) and the critical limit of 6.0. A high potassium level can cause dangerous heart rhythms, so it's reported first.

The pH of 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) and the PaCO₂ of 46 mm Hg (normal 35 to 45) are only slightly out of range and far from their critical limits (a pH below 7.20, a PaCO₂ above 65). A PaO₂ of 78 mm Hg is within the expected range for an adult over 65 (75 to 85), even though it's below the 80 to 100 expected for younger adults.

The pH of 7.34 isn't the right answer: it's out of range, but it's only mildly low; a potassium of 6.3 can cause dangerous arrhythmias, so it comes first.

Takeaway: Report a result past its critical limit first, such as a potassium level over 6.0 mmol/L, and compare the PaO₂ with the range for the client's age.

questions.stem: A client asks what cerebrovascular disease means. Which of the following conditions is a cerebrovascular disease?
options: Peripheral artery disease
Coronary artery disease
Carotid artery disease
Congestive heart failure
questions.rationale:
Cerebrovascular disease covers conditions that affect blood flow to the brain: stroke, a brain aneurysm, bleeding in the brain, and carotid artery disease, in which plaque narrows the carotid arteries in the neck that carry blood to the brain.

Peripheral artery disease narrows the arteries to the legs, coronary artery disease narrows the arteries to the heart muscle, and congestive heart failure is the heart's inability to pump blood effectively. All three are cardiovascular diseases, but none of them is a disease of the brain's blood supply.

Takeaway: Cerebrovascular disease affects blood flow to the brain: stroke, aneurysm, bleeding in the brain, and carotid artery disease.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing a 66-year-old client's health record. Which of the following findings are risk factors for cardiovascular disease?
options: Blood pressure of 152/94 mm Hg
Blood type O-positive, like both of the client's parents
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Smokes a pack of cigarettes a day
Father had a heart attack at age 50
Body mass index (BMI) of 34
questions.rationale:
Risk factors for cardiovascular disease include high blood pressure (152/94 is above the expected 120/80 or less), diabetes, smoking, a family history of heart disease, especially at a young age, and obesity (a BMI of 34 is above the expected 18.5 to 25). Others are high cholesterol, older age, and physical inactivity. Hypertension accounts for more deaths from cardiovascular disease in the United States than any other modifiable risk factor: a rise of 20 mm Hg in systolic pressure, or 10 mm Hg in diastolic pressure, doubles the risk of death from stroke or heart disease.

Blood type O-positive isn't a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

Blood type O-positive isn't the right answer: it's in the health record, but blood type isn't a risk factor for cardiovascular disease.

Takeaway: High blood pressure, diabetes, smoking, obesity, high cholesterol, inactivity, and family history raise the risk of cardiovascular disease; hypertension is the leading modifiable one.

questions.stem: A client is prescribed metoprolol for an arrhythmia. Which of the following antiarrhythmic classes does metoprolol belong to?
options: Class I: sodium channel blockers
Class II: beta blockers
Class III: potassium channel blockers
Class IV: calcium channel blockers
questions.rationale:
Metoprolol is a beta blocker, a class II antiarrhythmic: it blocks the sympathetic nervous system's effect on the heart, which slows the heart rate and conduction through the AV node.

Class I drugs, such as quinidine, block sodium channels. Class III drugs, such as amiodarone, block potassium channels. Class IV drugs, such as verapamil, block calcium channels.

Takeaway: Class I sodium channel blockers (quinidine), class II beta blockers (metoprolol), class III potassium channel blockers (amiodarone), class IV calcium channel blockers (verapamil).

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the fasting lipid results of 4 clients. Which of the following sets of results needs follow-up?
options: Total cholesterol 168 mg/dL, LDL 112 mg/dL
Total cholesterol 176 mg/dL, LDL 92 mg/dL
Total cholesterol 188 mg/dL, LDL 96 mg/dL
Total cholesterol 196 mg/dL, LDL 84 mg/dL
questions.rationale:
An LDL above 100 mg/dL is elevated, even when the total cholesterol is below 200 mg/dL. LDL is the cholesterol that builds plaque in the arteries, which leads to coronary artery disease and carotid artery disease, so an LDL of 112 mg/dL needs follow-up.

The other three clients have a total cholesterol under 200 and an LDL under 100. A total of 196 is close to the limit, but it isn't high, and that client's LDL of 84 is in range.

The highest total cholesterol, 196, isn't the right answer: it's under 200 with an LDL of 84; the LDL of 112 is the result above 100.

Takeaway: Check the LDL on its own: a total cholesterol over 200 mg/dL or an LDL over 100 mg/dL is high.

questions.stem: A client had several lymph nodes removed from under the right arm during cancer surgery and now has swelling of the right arm. Which of the following explains the swelling?
options: Less oxygen-rich blood reaches the arm
Extra tissue fluid can't drain back into the blood
The veins of the arm have lost their valves
The arm's capillaries can't exchange nutrients
questions.rationale:
Capillaries leak some fluid into the tissues, and the lymphatic system collects the extra and returns it to the blood, which keeps the fluid balanced and prevents edema. When lymph nodes and vessels are removed, extra tissue fluid can't drain from that area, so it builds up as swelling (lymphedema).

The surgery doesn't block the arteries, so oxygen-rich blood still reaches the arm. The veins keep their valves, and the capillaries still exchange oxygen and nutrients.

“The veins of the arm have lost their valves” isn't the right answer: failing valves also cause swelling, but here the lymph nodes were removed, so tissue fluid can't drain.

Takeaway: The lymphatic system returns extra tissue fluid to the blood; when it's damaged or removed, swelling follows.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the organs of the lymphatic system. For each function, click to specify the organ.
rows: Stores red blood cells and platelets
Filters lymph and holds immune cells along the lymphatic vessels
Helps recycle iron from old red blood cells
questions.rationale:
The thymus, in the upper chest, is where lymphocytes from the bone marrow mature into T lymphocytes (T cells). The spleen filters the blood, helps prevent infection, stores red blood cells and platelets, and takes part in iron metabolism by recycling the iron from old red blood cells. The lymph nodes sit along the lymphatic vessels; they filter lymph and hold immune cells, which is why they can swell during an infection and are checked in a lymph node exam.

The spleen fits two rows: it stores red blood cells and platelets and recycles iron from old red cells; T cells mature in the thymus.

Takeaway: Thymus: T cells mature. Spleen: filters blood, stores red cells and platelets, recycles iron. Lymph nodes: filter lymph.

questions.stem: After a heart attack, an area of a client's heart wall no longer contracts. Which layer of the wall was damaged?
options: The endocardium, the smooth lining inside the chambers
The myocardium, the thick muscle of the wall
The epicardium, the outer layer where the coronary arteries run
The fibrous pericardium, the tough sac around the heart
questions.rationale:
The myocardium is the cardiac muscle that contracts to pump blood. A heart attack (myocardial infarction) kills part of it, so that area no longer contracts.

The epicardium isn't the right answer: the coronary arteries that get blocked run along it, but the damage happens in the muscle they supply. The endocardium lines the chambers and valves, and the pericardium surrounds the heart.

Takeaway: Myocardium = the muscle that pumps. A myocardial infarction damages it.

questions.stem: A nurse measures a client's blood pressure as 136/84 mm Hg. The client asks, “What does the 84 mean?” Which response should the nurse give?
options: “It's the highest pressure in your arteries, while your heart squeezes.”
“It's the difference between the top and bottom numbers.”
“It's the lowest pressure in your arteries, while your heart relaxes and fills.”
“It's the average pressure your organs get over each whole heartbeat, top and bottom together.”
questions.rationale:
The bottom number is the diastolic pressure: the lowest pressure in the arteries, while the ventricles relax and fill between beats. The top number, the systolic pressure, is the peak while the ventricles contract.

“The average pressure your organs get” isn't the right answer: it sounds like a fuller answer, but that's the mean arterial pressure, which is worked out from both numbers. The difference between the numbers is the pulse pressure.

Takeaway: Systolic: the peak, during contraction. Diastolic: the lowest, during relaxation and filling.

questions.stem: A client with a low red blood cell count reports getting tired and short of breath while climbing stairs. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: “With fewer red blood cells, your blood carries less oxygen to your muscles.”
“With fewer red blood cells, your blood clots too slowly when you exert yourself.”
“With fewer red blood cells, you have fewer cells to fight off infections.”
“With fewer red blood cells, fluid leaks out of your blood vessels and into your lungs.”
questions.rationale:
Red blood cells carry oxygen on their hemoglobin. With fewer of them (anemia), the blood delivers less oxygen to working muscles, so exertion brings fatigue and shortness of breath.

“Fluid leaks into your lungs” isn't the right answer: it would explain the shortness of breath, but holding fluid in the vessels is albumin's job, not the red cells'. Clotting depends on platelets, and fighting infection on white blood cells.

Takeaway: Red blood cells carry oxygen; platelets clot; white blood cells fight infection; albumin holds fluid in the vessels.

questions.stem: An older adult stands up quickly after lying down. The blood pressure drops for a moment, and within seconds the heart rate rises and the blood pressure recovers. Which structures sensed the drop?
options: The kidneys, which release renin when blood flow to them falls
The baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
The chemoreceptors that sense oxygen and carbon dioxide in the blood
The hypothalamus, which releases more antidiuretic hormone
questions.rationale:
The baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch sense the stretch of the artery walls. When the pressure drops on standing, they send fewer signals to the medulla oblongata, which raises sympathetic activity: the heart speeds up and the vessels narrow, within seconds.

The kidneys aren't the right answer: renin raises blood pressure too, but the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system takes minutes to hours; a correction within seconds is the baroreceptor reflex. Chemoreceptors sense blood gases, and ADH acts more slowly.

Takeaway: Blood pressure changes within seconds: baroreceptors. Slower ones: the kidneys (RAAS) and ADH.

questions.stem: A client has had brief episodes of weakness in one arm, and an ultrasound shows a narrowed artery in the neck that supplies the brain. Which kind of cardiovascular disease does the client have?
options: Coronary artery disease
Peripheral artery disease
Cerebrovascular disease
Heart failure
questions.rationale:
A narrowed carotid artery, which supplies the brain, is a cerebrovascular disease, and brief episodes of one-sided weakness are warning signs of a stroke.

Peripheral artery disease isn't the right answer: the carotid is outside the heart, but that term covers the arteries to the limbs; arteries to the brain are cerebrovascular, and arteries to the heart muscle are coronary.

Takeaway: Coronary: the heart muscle. Cerebrovascular: the brain (like the carotids). Peripheral: the limbs.

questions.stem: A client has an inflamed pericardium, and each heartbeat now makes a scratchy sound. Which explanation of the pericardium's normal role should the nurse give?
options: The thick muscle layer of the heart that contracts to pump blood
The smooth inner lining of the heart that also covers the valves
A two-layer sac with fluid that lets the heart beat without rubbing
A flap of tissue that keeps blood moving forward through the heart
questions.rationale:
The pericardium is the sac around the heart: a tough fibrous outer layer and a serous layer with a small amount of fluid between its two sheets, so the heart can beat without rubbing. When it's inflamed, the roughened layers rub.

The smooth inner lining isn't the right answer: it's also a membrane, but that's the endocardium, inside the heart. The muscle layer is the myocardium.

Takeaway: Pericardium outside, myocardium in the middle, endocardium inside.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the heart's valves. For each item, click to specify the type of valve it describes.
rows: Held in place by chordae tendineae
questions.rationale:
The atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and mitral) sit between the atria and ventricles and are anchored by chordae tendineae; they close as the ventricles contract. The semilunar valves (pulmonic and aortic) sit where the ventricles empty into their arteries and close as the ventricles relax.

Calling the mitral valve semilunar because it's on the left with the aortic valve is a mistake. Mitral and tricuspid are both atrioventricular.

Takeaway: AV valves: tricuspid, mitral (chordae). Semilunar valves: pulmonic, aortic.

questions.stem: On a client's ECG, the P waves are missing, but each QRS complex is narrow and normal. Which part of the heart do these findings suggest isn't depolarizing in an organized way?
options: The atria
The ventricles
The heart valves
The pericardium
questions.rationale:
The P wave shows the atria depolarizing (just before they contract). Missing P waves mean the atria aren't depolarizing in an organized way; a normal, narrow QRS shows the ventricles are still depolarizing normally.

The ventricles isn't the right answer: they do the main pumping, but their wave, the QRS, is normal here.

Takeaway: P wave = atria; QRS = ventricles; T wave = ventricles recovering.

questions.stem: A nurse is matching the ECG to the heartbeat. For each event, click to specify the wave it goes with.
rows: The atria repolarize, hidden inside another wave
The pulse is felt just after this wave
questions.rationale:
The P wave: atria depolarize, then contract. The QRS complex: ventricles depolarize, then contract, which makes the pulse; the atria repolarize at the same time, hidden. The T wave: ventricles repolarize as they relax and refill.

Giving the atria's repolarization its own wave is a mistake. It happens during the much larger QRS, so it can't be seen.

Takeaway: Each wave is the electrical signal; the contraction follows it.

questions.stem: A client with kidney failure has a potassium level of 6.8 mmol/L, and the ECG shows tall, peaked T waves. Which part of the heartbeat does this finding suggest the potassium is affecting?
options: The atria's depolarization
The ventricles' repolarization
The closing of the semilunar valves
The filling of the coronary arteries
questions.rationale:
The T wave shows the ventricles repolarizing, and potassium is the key salt in repolarization. A high potassium makes the T waves tall and peaked (and can widen the QRS): a dangerous change to report right away.

The atria's depolarization isn't the right answer: it's another electrical event, but that's the P wave.

Takeaway: High potassium shows first in the T wave: the ventricles' repolarization.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the parts of the blood. For each item, click to specify whether it's part of the plasma or one of the formed elements.
questions.rationale:
Plasma (about 55%) is the liquid part: water carrying salts (sodium, potassium, calcium, and others), proteins (albumin, fibrinogen, and antibodies such as IgG and IgM), hormones, and vitamins. The formed elements (about 45%) are the cells and cell fragments: red cells, white cells, and platelets.

Putting antibodies with the white cells is a mistake, even though white cells make them. The antibodies themselves are proteins dissolved in the plasma.

Takeaway: Plasma: water, salts, proteins, hormones, vitamins. Formed elements: red cells, white cells, platelets.

questions.stem: A client's fibrinogen level is very low. Which finding should the nurse watch for?
options: Bleeding that's hard to stop
Swelling in both legs and feet
Frequent infections
Fatigue with exertion
questions.rationale:
Fibrinogen, a plasma protein made by the liver, becomes fibrin, the mesh that holds a clot together. Too little means clots form poorly, so bleeding is hard to stop.

Swelling isn't the right answer: it comes from a low plasma protein too, but that's albumin, which holds fluid in the vessels.

Takeaway: Low fibrinogen: bleeding. Low albumin: swelling.

questions.stem: A client's blood calcium level is low. Given calcium's roles in the blood, which problems should the nurse watch for?
options: Swelling of the legs from a low oncotic pressure
Frequent infections from too few antibodies
Shortness of breath from too few red blood cells
Muscle cramps and spasms, and slower clotting
questions.rationale:
Calcium, one of the plasma salts, is needed for muscle contraction and blood clotting. A low level makes nerves and muscles overexcitable (tingling, cramps, spasms) and can slow clotting.

Swelling from a low oncotic pressure isn't the right answer: it's another plasma problem, but oncotic pressure comes from albumin, not calcium.

Takeaway: Calcium: muscle contraction and clotting.

questions.stem: A nurse is checking a client's capillary refill. Which action is correct?
options: Press the skin over the shin for 5 seconds, and then check whether a pit remains
Count the pulse on the top of the foot for a full 30 seconds
Raise the leg and time how long it takes the foot to turn pale
Press the nail bed until it blanches, release, and time the color's return
questions.rationale:
Capillary refill tests peripheral perfusion, how well blood reaches the tissues: press the nail bed until it blanches, release, and time the return of color. Color back in about 2 seconds (no more than 3) is normal.

Raising the leg until it pales isn't the right answer: it's also a circulation check, but that's a test for arterial insufficiency, not capillary refill. Pressing the shin checks for pitting edema.

Takeaway: Capillary refill: press the nail bed, release, count the seconds.

questions.stem: Which findings should the nurse expect in a client with venous insufficiency of the legs?
options: Swelling that's worse at the end of the day
Brown discoloration of the skin around the ankles
Aching that eases when the legs are raised
A shallow, draining sore near the inner ankle
Weak or absent pulses on the top of the feet
Calf pain with walking that eases with rest
Feet that turn pale when raised
questions.rationale:
In venous insufficiency, leaky vein valves let blood pool: swelling by evening, brown skin around the ankles, aching that eases with elevation, and shallow, draining ulcers near the inner ankle.

Calf pain with walking and weak pulses don't fit venous insufficiency: they're leg circulation problems too, but they belong to arterial insufficiency, as does pallor when the feet are raised.

Takeaway: Venous: swelling, brown skin, relief with elevation. Arterial: claudication, weak pulses, pallor.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing clients' charts. Which clients are at higher risk of thrombus formation?
options: A client on bed rest for a week after surgery
A client who smokes and takes an estrogen birth control pill
A client who is dehydrated after days of vomiting
A client who walks 30 minutes a day and drinks plenty of water
A client who takes a daily aspirin as prescribed
A 25-year-old with a sprained wrist
questions.rationale:
Clots form when blood moves slowly (bed rest), when the blood clots too easily (estrogen, especially with smoking; dehydration, which concentrates the blood), or when a vessel wall is injured.

The daily aspirin isn't the right answer: it's a medication taken by people with heart disease, but aspirin makes platelets less sticky, lowering the risk. A sprained wrist doesn't slow blood flow in the legs.

Takeaway: Slow flow, easy clotting, and vessel injury cause thrombus formation.

questions.stem: A client with a deep vein clot in the calf suddenly becomes short of breath, with chest pain and a fast heart rate. Which explanation should the nurse give?
options: Part of the clot broke off and traveled to the lungs
The clot grew up the leg and is pressing on the heart
The clot is blocking air from reaching the lower lungs
The clot dissolved and released chemicals that tighten the airways
questions.rationale:
A thrombus stays where it forms; a piece that breaks off and travels is an embolus. From a leg vein, it travels through the right heart into the lung arteries, blocking blood flow there: sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, and a fast heart rate.

The clot growing up the leg isn't the right answer: clots can extend, but sudden lung symptoms point to an embolus that has already traveled.

Takeaway: A thrombus stays; an embolus travels (leg vein → lungs).

questions.stem: A 72-year-old client who smokes and has high blood pressure has a known abdominal aortic aneurysm. Which finding should the nurse report immediately?
options: A pulsing mass felt in the middle of the abdomen
Mild ankle swelling at the end of the day
Sudden, severe back pain with a falling blood pressure
A blood pressure of 148/88 mm Hg at a routine yearly visit
questions.rationale:
An aneurysm is a weak, bulging spot in an artery wall. Sudden severe back or abdominal pain with a falling blood pressure suggests it's rupturing, an emergency with heavy internal bleeding.

A pulsing abdominal mass isn't the right answer: it's a sign of the aneurysm, but in a client with a known aneurysm it's an expected finding, not a new emergency.

Takeaway: Aneurysm rupture: sudden severe pain and falling blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with diabetes has felt unusually tired, nauseated, and short of breath for the past hour, with no chest pain. Which condition should the nurse be concerned about?
options: A stroke, since she has no chest pain or pressure
A heart attack, which may cause no chest pain in some clients
An aneurysm, since nausea is the first and main warning sign of one
A murmur, since valve problems cause sudden nausea
questions.rationale:
A myocardial infarction happens when a blocked coronary artery starves heart muscle of oxygen. Women, older adults, and people with diabetes often have atypical symptoms: fatigue, nausea, and shortness of breath without classic chest pain.

A stroke isn't the right answer: it's another emergency, but stroke signs are face drooping, arm weakness, and speech trouble, which she doesn't have.

Takeaway: Heart attacks in women, older adults, and people with diabetes can be silent: think MI with sudden fatigue, nausea, and breathlessness.

questions.stem: A client's new murmur is caused by a mitral valve that doesn't close fully. Which explanation of the sound should the nurse give?
options: Blood leaking backward through the valve flows turbulently
The valve snaps shut too loudly with each heartbeat
Blood moves too smoothly through a valve that has become too wide
The pericardium rubs against the heart with each beat
questions.rationale:
A murmur is the sound of turbulent blood flow. A valve that doesn't close fully lets blood leak backward (regurgitation); a narrowed valve (stenosis) or a hole between chambers can also cause one.

The pericardium rubbing isn't the right answer: it also makes an extra sound, but that's a friction rub from an inflamed pericardium, not a murmur.

Takeaway: Murmur = turbulent flow: a leaky valve, a narrowed valve, or a hole.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing autonomic control of the heart and vessels. For each effect, click to specify the system that causes it.
rows: Slows the heart rate through the vagus nerve
questions.rationale:
The sympathetic system speeds up the heart, strengthens each beat (contractility), and narrows most vessels, so blood pressure rises. The parasympathetic system, through the vagus nerve, slows the heart, so blood pressure falls.

Giving the parasympathetic system the job of widening vessels directly is a mistake. Most vessels widen when sympathetic signals fall.

Takeaway: Sympathetic: faster, stronger, narrower, higher pressure. Parasympathetic: slower.

questions.stem: A client receives a medication that widens the arterioles. Which change in blood pressure should the nurse expect, and why?
options: It rises, because more blood can now flow through the vessels
It stays the same, because the heart rate rises to match
It rises, because the wider vessels can hold more blood
It falls, because wider vessels offer less resistance to flow
questions.rationale:
Blood pressure depends on how much blood the heart pumps and how much the vessels resist its flow. Widening the arterioles (a bigger caliber) lowers resistance, so the pressure falls.

It stays the same isn't the right answer: the heart rate often rises a little to compensate, but it doesn't fully offset the drop.

Takeaway: Wider vessels → less resistance → lower pressure; narrower → higher.

questions.stem: A client asks which foods fit a heart-healthy eating plan. Which of the following should the nurse include?
options: Cooking with extra-virgin olive oil
Oatmeal and brown rice
Skim milk and low-fat yogurt
Fresh vegetables seasoned with herbs
Cooking with coconut oil
Canned soups and deli meats
questions.rationale:
The instructor's heart-healthy habits: unsaturated fats (extra-virgin olive oil, avocado oil, other non-tropical vegetable oils), whole grains, low-fat dairy, and low sodium (fresh foods seasoned with herbs).

Coconut oil isn't the right answer: it's a plant oil, but it's a tropical oil, high in saturated fat. Canned soups and deli meats are high in sodium.

Takeaway: Unsaturated non-tropical oils, whole grains, low-fat dairy, low sodium.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing four clients' findings. Which client should the nurse identify as meeting the criteria for metabolic syndrome?
options: A man with a 36-in. waist, a blood pressure of 134/86 mm Hg, and an HDL of 52 mg/dL, who smokes
A man with a 42-in. waist, triglycerides of 190 mg/dL, and a fasting glucose of 108 mg/dL
A woman with a 33-in. waist, triglycerides of 140 mg/dL, and an HDL of 46 mg/dL
A woman with a fasting glucose of 112 mg/dL and an otherwise normal checkup
questions.rationale:
Metabolic syndrome is three or more of: a large waist (about 40 in. or more in men, 35 in. in women), triglycerides of 150 or more, a low HDL (under 40 in men, under 50 in women), a blood pressure of 130/85 or more, and a fasting glucose of 100 or more. The first man has three.

The woman with an HDL of 46 isn't the right answer: that's low for a woman, but it's her only criterion; her waist and triglycerides are within range.

Takeaway: Metabolic syndrome: 3 or more of waist, triglycerides, low HDL, blood pressure, and fasting glucose.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman's fasting lipid results are total cholesterol 186 mg/dL, LDL 92 mg/dL, and HDL 44 mg/dL. Which result should the nurse identify as a risk factor for cardiovascular disease?
options: The total cholesterol, since it's over 180 mg/dL
The LDL, since it's over 90 mg/dL
The HDL, since it's under 50 mg/dL for women
No result here is a risk factor
questions.rationale:
The instructor's cutoffs: total cholesterol over 200, LDL over 100, and HDL under 40 for men and 50 for women. Her total cholesterol and LDL are fine, but an HDL of 44 is low for a woman.

No risk factor isn't the right answer: it would be with the men's HDL cutoff of 40. Check the client's sex before reading the HDL.

Takeaway: HDL: under 40 (men) or under 50 (women) is a risk factor.

questions.stem: Click to highlight the findings in the nurses' notes that need follow-up.
questions.passage: Client reports [[cramping pain in the left calf after walking about 2 blocks, which eases after a few minutes of rest]]. [[Smokes 1 pack a day]]. [[Has type 2 diabetes]]. [[Left foot cool, pale, and shiny, with no hair]]; [[thick toenails]]. [[Weak (1+) pulse on top of the left foot]]. [[Capillary refill 4 seconds in the left toes]], [[2 seconds in the right toes]]. [[No swelling in either leg]]. [[A small, round sore with a pale base on the left little toe]].
questions.rationale:
Calf pain with walking that eases with rest (claudication), a cool, pale, hairless foot with thick nails, a weak pulse, a slow capillary refill, and a round, pale toe sore all point to poor arterial blood flow. Active smoking needs follow-up as a risk factor that can change.

Type 2 diabetes doesn't need follow-up today: it's a risk factor, but it's a known diagnosis in the history; the right toes' 2-second refill and the absence of swelling are normal.

Takeaway: Claudication, pallor, weak pulses, slow refill, and toe sores: arterial insufficiency.

questions.stem: For each finding, click to specify the problem it fits.
rows: Calf pain with walking that eases with rest
Weak pulse on top of the foot
A small, round toe sore with a pale base
Swelling that's worse at the end of the day
questions.rationale:
Arterial insufficiency: claudication, weak pulses, and deep, round, pale sores on the toes. Venous insufficiency: brown skin around the ankles and swelling by evening.

Calling any leg sore venous is a mistake, even though venous ulcers are common. A round, pale sore on a toe is arterial; venous ulcers are shallow, irregular, and near the inner ankle.

Takeaway: Sort leg findings into arterial (too little in) and venous (can't get out).

questions.stem: Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The client's findings most likely show {{0}} in the left leg, caused by {{1}}. When the leg aches at rest, the nurse should keep it {{2}}.

options: venous insufficiency
arterial insufficiency
a deep vein thrombosis
leaky valves in the leg veins
a clot in a deep leg vein
arteries narrowed by plaque
raised above the heart
level or slightly down
crossed at the knees

questions.rationale:
The findings show arterial insufficiency: plaque narrows the leg arteries (smoking, diabetes, high LDL, and high blood pressure all speed this up). Keeping the leg level or slightly down lets gravity help blood reach the foot.

Raised above the heart isn't the right answer: raising the legs helps swelling, but that's for venous problems; it makes arterial pain and pallor worse.

Takeaway: Arterial insufficiency: legs level or down, never raised.

questions.stem: Which teaching should the nurse include for this client?
options: Stop smoking, with help from a quit plan
Follow a heart-healthy diet with unsaturated fats and whole grains
Walk regularly, resting when the pain starts and then continuing
Check both feet each day for sores or color changes
Report a foot that suddenly turns cold, pale, or numb
Raise the legs on pillows to ease the pain
Soak the feet in hot water to improve circulation
questions.rationale:
Smoking, high LDL, low HDL, high blood pressure, diabetes, a BMI over 25, and age are the client's risk factors; quitting smoking and a heart-healthy diet address several. A walking program builds circulation, daily foot checks catch sores early, and a suddenly cold, pale limb is an emergency.

Soaking in hot water isn't the right answer: warmth seems to help circulation, but feet with poor blood flow (and diabetes) burn easily. Raising the legs worsens arterial pain.

Takeaway: Treat the risk factors, walk, protect the feet, and report a sudden cold, pale limb.

questions.stem: Three months later, the client returns. For each finding, click to specify whether it has improved, not changed, or gotten worse.
rows: Walking before calf pain starts: 2 blocks then, 5 blocks now
Smoking: 1 pack a day then, 1 pack a day now
Capillary refill, left toes: 4 seconds then, 4 seconds now
Toe sore: 0.5 cm across then, 1.2 cm across now
questions.rationale:
Walking farther before pain and a lower LDL show progress. The smoking and the slow capillary refill haven't changed, and the toe sore is larger: a wound that isn't healing because too little blood reaches it, which needs to be reported.

Calling the LDL normal now is a mistake. It's much better, but 104 is still just over the instructor's cutoff of 100.

Takeaway: Track each finding: improved walking and LDL don't offset a growing sore.

questions.stem: A client's heart valve doesn't close completely, so blood leaks backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium when the ventricles contract. Complete the following sentence.
questions.text: The leaking valve is the {{0}} valve, one of the {{1}} valves, which should close during {{2}}.

options: mitral
tricuspid
pulmonic
semilunar
atrioventricular
ventricular systole
ventricular diastole
atrial contraction

questions.rationale:
The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the tricuspid valve, one of the two atrioventricular (AV) valves. AV valves close when the ventricles contract (ventricular systole), so blood goes forward into the pulmonary trunk instead of back into the atrium.

The mitral valve isn't the right answer: it's the other AV valve, but it sits between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The semilunar valves (pulmonic and aortic) guard the exits of the ventricles and close in diastole, and during atrial contraction the AV valves are open, letting blood into the ventricles.

Takeaway: Tricuspid: right AV valve. Mitral: left AV valve. AV valves close in systole, semilunar valves in diastole.

questions.stem: After a heart attack, a client has crackles in both lungs and is short of breath when lying flat. Which part of the heart is most likely failing to pump out the blood returning from the lungs?
options: The left atrium
The left ventricle
The right ventricle
The right atrium
questions.rationale:
Blood from the lungs passes through the left atrium into the left ventricle, which pumps it out to the body. When a heart attack weakens the left ventricle, blood backs up into the lungs: crackles, and shortness of breath when lying flat (left-sided heart failure).

The left atrium isn't the right answer: it receives the blood from the lungs, but the chamber that pumps it out is the left ventricle. A failing right ventricle backs blood up into the body's veins instead, with swollen ankles and distended neck veins.

Takeaway: Left ventricle fails → blood backs up into the lungs; right ventricle fails → into the body's veins.

questions.stem: A client's ECG shows a regular rhythm at 50/min with no P waves before the QRS complexes. Complete the following sentences.
questions.text: The P wave normally shows the {{0}}. Without P waves, the {{1}} has most likely stopped firing, and the {{2}} has taken over pacing the heart.

options: ventricles depolarizing
ventricles repolarizing
atria depolarizing
AV node
SA node
bundle of His
AV node
Purkinje fibers
SA node

questions.rationale:
The P wave shows the atria depolarizing after the SA node fires. With no P waves, the SA node has most likely stopped, and the AV node, the next pacemaker, has taken over at its own slower rate of 40 to 60, which fits a rate of 50.

The AV node isn't the right answer for the second blank: the rate of 50 points to it, but it's the structure now pacing the heart, not the one that stopped. The QRS shows the ventricles depolarizing, and the T wave their repolarization.

Takeaway: P = atria depolarizing (from the SA node), QRS = ventricles depolarizing, T = ventricles repolarizing.
